summary: Describes the changes needed in the IPsec Security Policy Database and Security Association Database to support Robust Header Compression over IPsec. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: The rule books and address books for secret tunnels need new lines so that shortcut writing can be used.

questions: ipsec spd sad changes for rohc
how does rohc work with ipsec
subtitle: The database fields and packet-handling rules IPsec needs so that header compression can run inside protected tunnels.

tldr.problem: IPsec adds extra headers to every protected packet, and Robust Header Compression (ROHC) can shrink the inner headers, but IPsec has nowhere to store ROHC settings and no rules for mixing the two.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5858 adds ROHC parameters to the IPsec Security Policy Database and Security Association Database, a protocol identifier for compressed traffic, a second integrity check on decompressed headers, and rules for segmentation and nested IPComp.
tldr.outcome: A ROHCoIPsec implementation stays backwards-compatible with plain IPsec, and the Next Header value 142 marks packets that carry a ROHC header.

facts.label: Extra SAD item
facts.value: ROHC Data Item, inbound and outbound

today: RFC 5858 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2010. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be read together with the ROHCoIPsec framework in RFC 5856 and the IKEv2 extensions in RFC 5857.

sections.title: Why IPsec Needs Extensions for ROHC
sections.content:
IPsec protection gives IP traffic security services, but it costs extra packet headers. By compressing the inner headers, Robust Header Compression (ROHC) integrated with IPsec, called ROHCoIPsec, can reduce the overhead of IPsec-protected flows.

IPsec keeps its settings in two places. The Security Policy Database (SPD) says what services IP datagrams get. The Security Association Database (SAD) stores the parameters of Security Associations that have been set up. ROHC needs its own parameters in both.

On top of the database changes, the RFC requires three extensions to IPsec processing. ROHC packets must be identifiable, the integrity of a decompressed packet must be checkable, and the order of inbound and outbound steps must be fixed when IP Compression (IPComp), ROHC and IPsec are nested. The RFC also says these extensions have no implications for existing SPD fields or SAD parameters, so a ROHCoIPsec implementation is backwards-compatible with IPsec that does not support header compression.
sections.plainLanguage: Secret tunnels add a lot of extra writing on every letter. Shortcut writing can shrink it, but the tunnel's notebooks first need places to write down the shortcut rules.

sections.title: New SPD Fields
sections.content:
When the processing action for a set of selectors is PROTECT, the SPD processing info is extended with ROHC channel parameters.

  • MAX_CID: the highest context ID the local decompressor will handle. It MUST be at least 0 and at most 16383, and 0 means one context.
  • MRRU: the size of the largest reconstructed unit the local decompressor should reassemble from ROHC segments. Because in-order delivery of ROHC packets cannot be guaranteed, it SHOULD be set to 0, which means no segment headers are allowed on the channel.
  • PROFILES: the list of ROHC profiles the local decompressor supports, taken from the ROHC profile identifiers registry.

A ROHC integrity algorithm list and a ROHC ICV length MUST also be present. The algorithms that MUST be supported are the authentication algorithms listed in RFC 4835 (or its successor).

Two ROHC parameters are left out because they are set implicitly. LARGE_CIDS follows from MAX_CID (if MAX_CID is 15 or less it is assumed to be 0). FEEDBACK_FOR points at the ROHC channel of the SA in the reverse direction; if there is no such SA, ROHC MUST NOT operate in bi-directional mode.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule book gets new lines such as how many different conversations the shortcut reader can follow, and which shortcut styles it knows.

sections.title: The ROHC Data Item in the SAD
sections.content:
Unless a field is marked populate-from-packet, SAD entries are filled in from the matching SPD entries when the SA is created. To support ROHC, the SAD gains a ROHC Data Item on both inbound and outbound SAs.

The item holds the channel parameters MAX_CID, PROFILES and MRRU. On an inbound SA they describe the local decompressor; on an outbound SA they describe the local compressor. Both directions MUST also store the ROHC integrity algorithm, its key and the ICV length, which are used to verify headers after decompression.

Inbound SAs MUST additionally carry FEEDBACK_FOR, a reference to a ROHC channel in the opposite direction between the same endpoints. An inbound and an outbound channel MAY be coupled into a bi-directional ROHC channel.

The values MAY be set by hand for manual SAs, or through a key exchange protocol such as IKEv2 that has been extended to signal ROHC parameters (RFC 5857).
sections.plainLanguage: Each tunnel's address book entry gets a small card listing its shortcut settings and a secret code word used to double-check the result.

sections.title: Marking Compressed Traffic
sections.content:
A "ROHC" protocol identifier marks header-compressed traffic on a ROHC-enabled SA. If an outbound packet has a compressed header, the Next Header field of the security protocol header (AH or ESP) MUST be set to the ROHC identifier. If ROHC did not compress the header, the field does not hold that identifier. On the inbound side, the Next Header value MUST be checked to decide whether ROHC decompression is needed.

IANA allocated the value 142 to ROHC in the Protocol Numbers registry for this purpose.

Using the identifier for anything other than ROHCoIPsec is currently not defined. Any future use would need a specification of the logical compression channel and a study of the security considerations outside the Next Header field of security headers.
sections.plainLanguage: A little sticker on the envelope says whether the letter inside was written in shortcut, so the receiver knows whether to expand it.

sections.title: Checking Decompressed Headers
sections.content:
ROHC is inherently lossy: significant reordering or loss between ROHC peers can cause undetected decompression failures, where wrong packets are forwarded into the protected domain. To guard against this, ROHCoIPsec MAY compute a second Integrity Check Value (ICV) with an extra integrity algorithm and key. This ROHC ICV MUST be computed over the uncompressed IP header, the higher-layer headers and the payload, and it is appended to the compressed packet.

The decompressor recomputes the value over the decompressed packet, not including the authentication data, and compares it to the appended ICV. If they differ, the packet MUST be dropped.

The order of steps is fixed. Outbound: compute the ICV on the uncompressed packet, compress the headers, append the ICV, then apply AH or ESP. Inbound: apply AH or ESP, remove the ICV, decompress, compute an ICV on the decompressed packet, then compare. A mismatch means the packet MUST be dropped; otherwise IPsec processing resumes.
sections.plainLanguage: Before shrinking a letter you write a secret checksum number. After the receiver expands it, they work out the number again, and if it does not match, they throw the letter away.

sections.title: Segmentation, Tunnel MTU and Nested IPComp
sections.content:
RFC 4301 already says what to do when an outbound packet exceeds the SA path MTU. For ROHCoIPsec there is one change: since current ROHC profiles cannot compress IP fragments, pre-encryption fragmentation MUST NOT happen before ROHC processing.

If a compressed packet is still too big and the MRRU is non-zero, ROHC segmentation MAY be used, and it MUST occur before AH or ESP processing. The RFC does not recommend it, because in-order delivery of segments is not guaranteed. Each segment gets its own AH/ESP sequence number, incremented by one per segment, and the ROHC ICV is appended to the compressed packet before segmenting, not to each segment. If the implementation lacks a path MTU estimate, it SHOULD NOT attempt to segment.

For nested use with IPComp, the outbound order is: compute the ICV and apply ROHC, apply IPComp, then apply the security protocol. Inbound is the reverse: IPsec processing, IPComp decompression, then ROHC decompression and integrity verification.
sections.plainLanguage: If a shortened letter still does not fit in the mailbox, you may cut it into numbered pieces. The RFC says that is risky, because the pieces might arrive out of order.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The strength of the integrity algorithm used to verify decompressed headers matters. A weak check raises the chance that a wrongly decompressed packet is forwarded into the protected domain.

ROHCoIPsec may also make traffic flow analysis easier. An attacker watching the sizes of encrypted packets might spot a new flow, for example a group of long packets followed by many short ones. ROHC padding can randomize packet sizes to counter this, but it reduces the efficiency gained from header compression.
sections.plainLanguage: A weak double-check lets a garbled letter slip through, and the sizes of shortened letters can give clues about what is going on, unless you pad them out.
